Had none fallen in the affray but the real rioters who were personally engaged in the attack on the theatre and its legal deb niff rs ; however, much the destruction of human life might be deplored, a certain justice in ibe extent would strike every mind and strengthen the satisfaction natural to the lover of order, when law triumphs over wanton and brutal violence, liut on such an occasion the innocent and the guilty are struck dow n together, and however riecessaiy the victory, there is something inexpressibly painful ur its cost. It is urged by many that Mr. Macreadv should not have appeared on Thutsday night after having been driven front the st ge on Monday. We do not ste the justice of that argument. He had been driven fiom the stage by a gang of ruffians : he was asked to return to it by some ol our most estimable citizens. He was right in following their request, and it was the duty of the authorities

to protect him in so doing. Else of wlml use are authorities at all ! If it please a rn<d> to declare that an obnoxious newspaper si all not appear, is its publisher to submit to such dictation? No freeman will say yes, but till will applaud and uphold the resolution which maintain the freedom of the press to the last. The two cases are precisely of the same kind. Every man exercising a lawful vocation has a claim to the whole pioleciion of Society. Still we do Mr. Macrcndy the justice to believe that had lie had any reason to anticipate the death of u single person as the consequence of iris second appearance ii would never have taken place. The spirit of bravado and provocation certainly do. s not appear in the note with which he teplied to the letter requesting him to commence his performances ; he had no desire for a repetition of lire disagreeable events of Monday, still less any conception that the fury of his opponents could result in bloodshed. Scenes like that of that terrible niglii are, thank (jnd ! too raie in this count is to tender the expectation of them natural or easy, þÿ YVe knew Unit the military had been moored out, but did not believe that they would bo necessary. We thought the Police backed by a large number of peaceable citizens, who we knew would be present, would bo able to quell with promptness, 'vital disorder might be attempted. doubt it was that of Mr. Macie.adv It ,s impossible to remove the disgrace which the tint has lived upon (lie City through the eon. venienl charge of impropriety or wrong judgment on Ins part, or the crime ol those who began and continued it.

From Wilmer and Smith's European Times, July 2, 1849. AUSTRIA AND HUNGARY. In the south of Hungary two actions have happened, and have boih terminated to the advantage of the imperialists. The Hungarian general, Perezel, from the fortress of Peterwardein, made an attack on some Austrian intrenchments, but was ultimately repulsed, and driven with loss into Peterwarden. though the Austrians admit that their own troops suffered severely. The other battle was fought bv the Han JcHachich. and is assenedio have been a brilliant victory; but the Austrian accounts are evidently not trustworthy, at least as regards their own losses. From the official account in the VVienei Zeiturig, it appears that the ban left Tittel enliven the 5th June, and marching at the head of eight brigades, horse and foot, advanced to the Homan entrenchments, where he proceeded to dispose his troops in ndvan tageous positions On the 7th an Hungarian

army of 13 battalions and il ice laiteri-s came down upon him. and in the engagement which ensued it is supposed that the Hunga. rians fired their artillery tort high, for none of their halls took effect. The Ausliian aitille ry, on trie contrary, did great execution in the Hungarian ranks, so much so. indeed, that the imperialist general, Hettinger, was ena bled to make a cavalry attack, break through their line of hanle, and cause the precipitate flight of the dismayed Magyais Two of their battalions were cut to pieces, so that the Hungarians had 500 killed and 220 dangerously wounded, most of ihe latter being sacrificed to the passions of the infuriated imperialists. In short, the loss of the Magyars, as given by.jhe If iener Zeitung, is no less than 1500 killed; while so wonderful were the manoeuvres of General Oettinger, that on v two imperialists were killed, and 10 or 12 wounded. The advices of the I6th from Vienna make mention of a tremendous encounter with the Hungarians. The Austuans and Kussians are said to have been completely defeated, and to have left on the field the fabulous number of 23 000 killed. This battle took place on the 13th. 14th, and 15th, in the large plain between Kaub and Weiselburg. It lasted 01 bouts. The loss of the Magyars is stated at 8000 The Austrians were commanded by Uaynau, the Kussians by Kudiger, and the Hungarians by Gem gey. Although the news of this battle has been received in private letters, singularly enough no paper alludes to it. The Lloyd, of Vien-

na, contains not the most distant allusion to it. RUSSIA AND CIRCASSIA. Prom Bell's Weekly Messenger, London , May 21, 1849. We have the satisfaction to state, that the British Cabinet, under a due conviction of the awful state of the Continent, and under an equally sound conviction, that the peace of Europe can never he restored, unless there be a thorough union of all the Continental Sovereigns and their armies, to act together for the suppression of universal þÿanarchy has at length accepted two important proposals trom these Sovereigns; viz., that the Danish war shull be concluded bv agreeing to the proposition of the Danish government,

that there shall be a terns rare and provisignal division of the duchy of Schleswig; the half of it to be ceded to die Get manic Union, the other half to remain in possession of the Crown of Denmark ; the taxes, crown rents, and other royalties of both parts still indeed to belong to the King of Denmark, but the ceded part, as to all war levies, and os to any participation in foreign wars or diplomacy, to be subject to the laws of any Ger man Union, which shall be accepted by Austria, Prussia, and the other sovereigns of Germany in their character of a Germanic corporation. We cannot conceive anything better calculated to put a satisfactory end to this Danish war, and to t tie consequent division of the Royal armies of Germany, the entire union of which is so absolutely required to oppose the present sweeping current of popular anarchy. It is only by such a union of the total forces of the confederated sovereigns, that any reasonable expectation can be entertained of the suppression of the present social anarchy, and that these populous nations can be restored to the authority of law and government. > The second proposition, which has also doubtless proceeded from the voluntary act ot the same Sovereigns, and which is now understood lo have been accepted by our government, is, that We shall so far withdraw our recognition from (tie Central Government of the Frankfort Assembly, as to recal our ambassador Irom that station, and without any offensive act dispense with the fur-

ther residence of any accredited representative of the Frankfort government at our own Court. It was stated by Austria and Prussia, that they themsehes had found it necessary to disavow the lesal and constitutional competency of the Frankfort Assembly, and more especially since their promolitation of a genera! constitution lor all Germany, without awaiting the express consent of the several sovereigns composing the Germanic body. þÿ It is concluded, therefore, and very justly, that our further acknowledgment of the Frankfort Assembly would amount to an unauthorised recognition of a body disavowed by their own Sovereigns; a body also already proceeding to the usurpation of the powers of government. Under these representations, it is understood that Lord Cowley, our Minister acting at Frankfort, has been recalled by the Biitish Cabinet. It is a further consequence nt those two important measures, that an immediate alliance will be made, on the pnrt of all the German suveromps, for their common defence against the insurrectionary movements of ti e people in the several States of Germany, and then an immediate declaration will, we presume, tie issued against the Fianklort Assembly in particular, in which this Assembly will be proclaimed to he an illegal body, and the members of it will he commanded to dissolve, and to return into the states ol their respective sovereigns. i. . . þÿ ... The objects of the contest are the Duchies of Sleswiok and Holstein. This almost every body knows But how the. war coiiid arise is not so obvious. It is even an enigma to a great many people in Germany, as well ns in Denmark ; and surely it is not to be wondered if in other countries the people should be ignorant of the real state of facts. When we consider that þÿSlesanck formerly called South Jutland þÿ forming a natural part of the great Danish peninsu a Jutland, has been a Danish province ever since the existence of tire kingdom of Denmark ; and that Holstein has belonged to this kingdom for four hundred years ; þÿ when we farther consider that Denmark, since the days of Charlemagne, has never acted in hostility against Germany, or made any attempt to encroach upon Iter rights, and that, on the other hand, the King of Denmark, as sovereign of Holstein, has always scrupulously fullilled his obligations to the German confederation þÿ and finally, when we consider that the great majority of the people of Holstein, as well as of Sleswiok, have never harbored the desire to be torn from Denmark jand incorporated with Germany ; the origin of the present war may truly appear mysterious. The facts contained in the following sketch are derived from an intelligent gentleman who resided many years in those countries, and has no predilection, he says, either lor Danes or for the Germans.

Germany, until 1806 an Empire, and since 1815 a Confederation, contains a number of separate Slates, independent in their local affairs, and united only for the purpose of mutual safety and defence. Thus, for instance, if the French should invade the Grand Duchy of Baden, it would be considered an attack upon the whole German Confedesa lion, and all the other German States would be obliged to assist Baden in defence. In this sense Holstein has always formed part of the German Empire, as well as of the German Confederation, without prejudice to its governmental connection w ith Denmark. Holstein is in the same political condition us Hanover was from 1714 until 1837, during

Holstein is situated between the Elbe and | Empire for many hundred years, the Eider ; which latter river forms, and i into the possession of the French in the six since the days of Charlemagne has constantly : teenth, seventeenth and eighteenth centuries; formed, the Northern boundary not only of Holstein but of this part of Germany. Charlemagne conquered the country, and it after- | 1 tic, wards formed part of the old celebrated duchy of Saxony until the beginning of the 12th century, when the courts of Schaeunburg or Schaumburg were invested with Holstein as a fief. These remained in pos session of it until 1458, when the last male descendant, Count Adolphus XII , died childless. His only heiress was his sister, the Countess of Oldenburg, whose eldest son, Christian, had ascended the throne of Den mark in 1418, and who now, after the death ' 1 of Count Adolphus XIL, also inherited Hob stein. i In this way Holstein (since 1471 endowed with the title of Duchy) came into connec. tion with Denmark. Unfortunately, the succeeding Danish Kings did not exercise their governmental power in Holstein directly, but by vassals, Vm ic. by were younger princes of the royal family, invested with the duchy as a fief. The grandson, Feter, ascended the Russian throne, and bequeathed the duchy of Holstein to his son Paul, (sub sequcntly Emperor Russia,) of who in 1773, ceded all his rights in it to the crown of Denmark. Since that time the duchy has been again ruled directly by the kings of Denmark. The present king, Frederik VII, has no children yet, and perhaps may die without any. Through the favor of a correspondent at Rio Janeiro we have been furnished with the Jornatdo Comercie of April 22, from which we translate for The Tribune the following account of a serious riot which took place at Santa Ciitharina, a small sea port on the island of the same name, some distance south of Rio: We have heaid of some lamentable scenes at Santa Catharina, between the populace and a large number of the American endgiants for California, who touched at the pott for water and provisions. These have been carried to bloodshed to both sides, and the death of one of the Americans. A letter from that port on the 18th gives the follow ing particulars: " Eight American vessels, on their way to California, with from 700 to 800 passengers on board, have touched here. On Sunday, the 15th, a number of them, while on shore, committed some disorders. The natives, who had shown hostility toward them from from the day of their landing collected in groups, armed themselves and attacked the disorderly characters. These also took arms: a fight then occurred, in which one American was killed and four severely wounded, us well as about the same number of natives " The disorder had hardly commenced, when the President ordered out the whole police force, the infantry and the National Guard. Pursued with loss, the Americans look refnao in a hotel and there continued to tight. The armed force surrounded the hotel, which next day surrendered at the command

of Hie authorities. In the alarm caused by the Cholera this fatal follyis carried to intolerable exeess. People think they may fall sick, or fancy they are so already, and tush to buy and swallow the last nostrum which tliey have seen advertised in the papers, or which is paiaded in staring handbills along the streets. Y\ ho knows what amount of pills, panaceas, purges, and other diabolical inventions, not lit to be pitched into a common sewer, have been forced down the innocent throats of frightened simpletons in this city within the past foitnight. We say to all parties: Leave Physic alone. Don't convert yourselves into short-lived depositories of quack medicines, whether prescribed by the regular or irregular (acuity. Russian Vengeance. Behind the chapei was a rack, and on both sides of the rack were several rows of gallows. some miles in length, and instruments of torture ready for the unfortunate victims. The punishments were in accordance with the degree of culpability and station in society of the rebels. In the first row of gallows the most guilty were executed ; after being subjected to the rack, they were quartered alive 'flic leaders had their right hand and left leg cut off, and were afterwards impaled on long spikes, and left to their horrible late. Their groans weie heard for miles, and their bodies feasted the eyes of the panic-stricken population. In the second row of gallows they were only quartered, and their sufferings were at least shorter. In the third row, the parties were simply beheaded. In the fourtli row, they were merely hanged. þÿ In the fifth, they ran the gauntlet and the knout. All the ecclesiastics were burned. There were separate gallows for women, married and maiden. Even children, from thirteen yeais. were subjected to great cruelty. þÿ AI amed couples were occasionally hanged on the same gallows, ns well as whole Inmilies. During the space of three months 13.000 human beings were executed in the presence of Dolgorouki. Stenko Bazin's nephew and his particular friend were quartered. Among the female prisoners there was a handsome nun, who, over her female garments, had a male attire. She commanded a corps of 7000 men, cave rhore than once proofs of extraordinary courage and great

ability in the field, and inflicted terrible losses on the Bussians. As for a nun in Bussia to run away from a monastery is a capital offence, she lay down quietly on a funeral pile, and was hurried to ashes. WESTERN AFRICA. An expedition, conducted by Major S. J. Hill, of 2nd West India regiment, wei|t up the Gambia in the beginning of May, to inflict punishment on a native King who had grossly insulted the British flag, in the person of the Governor, Mr. R G Macdonnell. The Morning Herald publishes a letter Irom an officer engaged in it. About 200 troops, with 33 pensioners, and 32 military men, formed the brigade, which was provided with one howitzer, two six pounder field guns and three rocket guris. The expedition sailed 70 miles up the Gambia, when they disembarked, and marched into the interior. On the 6th of May they succeeded in burning the fortified town of Hambacoo, though not, it appears, without considerable difficulty, having first tried to make a breach in the place, and then to storm it. without effect They then proceeded to Keerning, the capital of the native prince, part of which they burnt, but did not succeed in taking it, finding it (the writer says) impracticable. They then determined to return, which they did without much loss, though continually Imrrassed by the enemy. The English loss was-five men killed, and two officers and twenty men wounded This is the first military expedition which has ever been into the interior of the Gambia, and returned in good order. þÿ W'illmer <$ Smith's European Times.

THE AVARICIOUS BAKER. At a late missionary meeting in England, a speaker related the following anecdote, in illustration of his remark that "avarice never prospered any people:" lie remembered a baker that was very niggardly, and lie was desirous of enlarging his oven. Well, how to do this on economical principles was the desideratum. I' ire bricks were costly, too costly. What could lie gel ? Ob, he had it ! There were some grave stones which, if he could nicely get hold of, would suit well. Could he get them snugly, the job would soon be done þÿ No matter how, hut he got hold of them and immediately set to work at his oven. He enlarged it, and ll i trued n with the fragments of grave stones; hut, without thought, placed the lettered sides up. The ' baking their he day' took place. His neighbors bought hut loaves. Mind, they were not in tins, were oven bottom loaves, that is. the dough baked on the oven bottom, without tins. They were duly baked. The neighbors fetched the foaves, but, astonishment þÿI What magic! On one loaf was, depnited ' this life,' on another, aged 70 years,' and ' so on. The tale soon got out, and the baker was never troubled to bake another loaf, and soon was ruined. His covelousness punish ed itself, and so it would he with all those professing but not acting with that liberality that become Christians.

Sir, þÿ Cholera having now assumed a frightful prevalence among all classes, wiibout respect to locality, I wish, in trespassing upon your columns, to guatd the public against ridiculous nostrums, and to disabuse their minds of the idea that the treatment adopted in the East with success can be here, where not only the climate but the constitutional habits of the people are so widely different, attended with the same advantages; whilst 1 lav before them the prevention of the disease, and a series of remedies at once prompt, practical, and efficient, for its treatment and cure þÿ promising that such are founded upon an extensive experience and careful observation of the course and character of the disease in the years 1832, 1833 1848, and are identical with thoe given in my evidence before the sanitary commissioners, and so strongly recommended bv them in their report presented to both houses of parliament: the efficacy of which treatment has been fully proved, on an extensive scalewithin the last week, both in my private practice as well as amongst the police forcet and other public institutions to which 1 am attached. Prevention þÿ Prevention is physical and moral. Moral prevention consists in the avoiding of all conceits of the disease, and needless alarms at its progress. The surest agent to ellect this is a firm belief that cholera is in no wise contagious, and that it can be disnimed of ail its virulence by a timely and judicious treatment. 1'hysical prevention

divides itself into what food is to be taken or rejected, and what habits of life are to be followed or omitted. 1 recommend the use of comfortable and nutritious animal food of the solid kind, rice well boiled, warm clothing, and free ventilation. 1 deprecate the use of spirituous and fermented liquors (except a limited allowance of port, sherry, or brandy and water to those whose digestion requires it), fruit, raw vegetables, strong purgative medicines, and of shell and salt fish. þÿ Finally, strongly I advise the observance of regular and early hours, the avoidance of intemperate excesses, and a strict attention to cleanliness, as well personal as local ; the latter, being in a great measure dependent upon the public large at rather than upon individuals is to be secured by tfie municipal and parochial authorities taking care to have the sewers well flushed, and tiie squalid dwellings of the poor lime washed. The Premonitory Stage and its Treatment þÿ So far as my observation extended ni the periods before mentioned, 1 found that spasmodic cholera, with few exceptions, was preceded by certain premonitory symptoms of which diarrhoea, or purging, was the most promiinwit, but which symptom was too often overlooked by those laboring under the at tack. It, therefore, becomes of vital importnn-te that every case of purging which may occur should be without loss of time arrested in its progress ; for so fully convinced am 1 of the benefits resulting from a prompt atten-

tion to howel complaints, that 1 believe that the actual choleric symptoms may, in the inajoiuy of cases, tie thereby prevented þÿ the li ves of thousands. 'I he pmging is for the most part accompanied by nausea, followed by a sense of heat and weight in the stomach, slight cramp in the

When sickness with derangement of the bowels is felt, the patient (if an adult) should mix a lablespootdu! of mustard or double that quantity ol common salt in half-a pint of warm water, a third part of either to be taken every ten minutes and free vomiting be produced. Alter the stomach has been cleansed out with more warm water, 20 drops of tincture of opium should be given in a glass of brandy and water, to be followed up witlt a pill, compos ed 6f five grains of calomel and two grains of opium ; smaller doses in the proportion of two grains of calomel and a quarter grain of opium to be taken at intervals of every two hours until the bile is observed to pass in the evacuations. In the event of children being attacked with bowel complaints of this kind, they should have administered to them, in proportion to their age, one or two teaspoonfuls of tfie chalk mixiuie, the formula of which 1 shall give below, and one giuin of calomel every two hours, until the same effect (the passing of bile) be visible in the evacuations. Families should have in readiness a mixture of the following form Fiepared chalk, half an ounce; powdeied gum of acacia, half an ounce; opiate confection, one diachm ; aromatic confection, two diachms : tincture of catechu, one ounce ; white sugar, two drachms ; salvolatile, two drachms ; cinnamon or peppermint water, a half pint; þÿ of which mixture an adult may take three

tablespovufuls after each disoiuered motion. I also strongly advise the use of an embrocation of heated turpentine to be rubbed over tiie bowels and extremities to which the addition of one third part of laudanum would i.e a most important improvement. Lhould the ingredients of this embrocation not be at hand, mustard poultices ought to be placed over the whole extent of Hie ubdutr-m , and common wine bottles, or stone jar n.icd with hot water and rolled in flannel be applied lo at the stomach and feet. It the «|<u intent be ail eligible the patient should not 1 re- moved, but be kept in a petlectly !,. >;/,ontal position, as any attempt to sit uptight might prove fatal. The patient will experience a great relief from cramps by havmg a band age tightly tied round the seat of pain, and should tins piuve inefficient I can, from recent experience in private practice duiing the current year, speak highly ol chloroform as a most efficient agent in removing choleric spasm þÿ from two to five drops of it being administered in a little ginger tea, or any other warm fluid. From the St. Thomas Times, July 28, 1849. To the Editor of the St. Thomas Times. Mr. Editor ! Permit me sir to say, that in perusing your last number, I was vastly astonished at your having inserted the speech of our most gracious Sovcieign on the occasion of the disso lotion of the I >iet, without paying it a single laudatory liibute under the head of an edito. rial, in particular as you are in the habit of praising or commenting on the speeches of foreign tnonarchs. 1 am thoroughly convinced it is not at all owing to disrespect or from not participating in the' joy and exultation thai the great work, our glorious con siitution, of which the speech of our Sovereign is, as it were, the key stone, has diffused in every loyal breast; but 1 am induced to believe, that in consequence of the press being subject to a hug hear, you are apt to be remiss in your duty as an Editor, in all civilized countries an honourable and responsible office I However commendable it may be to prefer silence to having one's productions " torn up in rags,' I am yet of opinion, that the good light yught not to be given up without a struggle. Having called your attention to the omission in your last paper, I trust sir, that in your next number you will make ample amends by favoring your subset ibers w i i h an article suitable to the soul stirring event of 1 Jen mark being de facto and dr. jure a constitutional monarchy, in which article no doubt, too will in voui usual graphic manner siale what is i he wish of every raiional being in our

roinmnnriy, wlvo does not consider loaves and fishes" to be the principal ingredients of life that we. His Majesty's transatlantic subject should partake of the irghis and pri- Tuteges granted to our fortunate brethren in the mother country. 1 am, Sir, Your obedt. servant, NIL DF.SPKKANDUM. St. Thomas, 23id July 18J9.

3 'jr. 0 :ii OIZ A T J. 3. Nil Dbsi ukanhum is perfectly well aware that fettered as our Colonial J'ress is by the law of censorship, we are hound to he especially guarded in commenting on state papers which effect solely the mother country. The Pi ess is not subject to a bug bear, but it is subject to an existing law, and must conform to it until repealed. We preferred silence on principle, for while we rejoiced most sin cerely that our Gracious Monarch had signalized his reign by elevating his subjects in Europe from serfs to citizens and free men, we could not but sympathise with the thousands of his loyal Colonial subjects who are deeply grieved that the same blessing has not been extended to them We considered on mature reflection it wiser to be silent. The speech spoke for itself þÿ no laudatory of ours was required, it would have been tantamount to holding a candle to the sun we were hy no means afraid of having our production torn up in rags, especially, if it had been worthy of the compliment JXil Desperandum lias been pleased to pay us, i. e , " in our usual graphic manner." We must confess we do not exactly understand the application of the pluase þÿ does J\il Desperandum mean that we were afraid of having an article on the subject " torn to rags" prior to publication, or subsequently by criticism? þÿ if the former, wc must confess it, but if the laticr, most certainly not þÿ "discretion is the better part of valor," and silence sometimes more poient than eloquence. The masses in this

California. þÿ Letter from Governor Smith. þÿ A gentleman in this city lias received a private letter bv the last steamer, dated at San Francisco, California, from the gallant and meritorious Major General 1'ersifor F. Smith commanding the 3d, or Pacific division of the United States Army ; which, although not intended to meet the public eye, we deem so highly interesting that we have extracted several paragraphs for publication þÿ the gen tlemnn yielding to our wishes in that respect. " You only think of California in connexion with gold; and, indeed, a most wonderful connexion il is. As to the extent of country holding the precious metal, and the comparative facility with which it is procured, there has been no exaggeration. The whole slope of the Sierra Nevada, on the western side, for a length of more than 400 miles, and in a belt of at least 40, contains il in greater or smaller quantities ; and it rnav extend still further ii research is made. It is found simply by digging and washing the earth ; no ex pensive machinery and no intricate chemical process are necessaiy to develope the magic board A pickaxe, shovel, or even a but

cher s Unite, mo; < n me enttn arm stone and the most simple basin for w ashing, have been as tidily rewaided as the most appiov ed machines from other counties. Good luck in the laborer choosing his location, has more than compensated for want oi sk li The real ditlieuliies lie in the hardships to be encountered, in the remote uninhabited spots where I lie gold is found. Want of lood, over woi king excited by success, bad waier exposure and dissipation, all combine to exact a heavy tiibute for the wealth when found. All are riot successful, but every one works on, hoping that the next blow of his pick will disclose a treasure that will surpass all be has hitherto heard of Many die unheeded, many come off sick ; but theie are ten arriving from each quarter of the globe to replace every one who goes. Chinese, Sandwich Islanders, Chilians, Peruvians, Prussians, Mexicans, French, English, Irish, outnumber as yet the Americans, but the latter will soon have their share. Provisions, woolen clothing, liquors, kitchen and mining utensils, sell at enormous profits in the mines; other articles scarcely sell at all. Woman's gear is altogether a drug. " The amount of gold hitherto found s hardto determine. It is ssidahout $4,000,000 have been expoited. 1 shall be able in a few weeks, from facts 1 am collecting, to make some approximation to it. " in the mean time, all this is disastrous for us. No servants are to be bad; £25(1 a month has been refused in my presence by a cook. All my servants have quit, and yes

terday I engaged one at $100 a month, became he is too sick to go to the mines, hot I shall certainly loose him il he gels his health " 1 he quartermaster pays $5000 a year for the house 1 live in, and it would make a poor toll house for a country bridge. The climate is cold all the year round, and foggy in the summer. The lulls ate bare, an t the country is all þÿbills (forgive the bull) The heel is execrable, and vegetables þÿ none : and nobody has time to catch fish, if there are any þÿ voila la cart". " Any one who will come here to dig gold, or bring goods with him to sell to the diggers, will make money. No other business will succeed. " 1 » ' 1 ' "U STEAM UMJIAE, The following account of the parts of the steam engine is intended, without, entering into minute practical details, still fully to explain the principle or gcneial nature of the machine. It should serve to render very interesting to an attentive reader, a visit to any place where a steam engine is in use ; and it should make evident the folly of many of the modern schemes for improving the engine. The part which first claims attention, is the great barrel, constituting the centre or main portion of the machine, in which the pinion is moved up and down by the action of steam entering alternately above and below it, through the pipes. The barrel, or cylinder, is bored with extreme accuracy, and the piston is padded round its edge with hemp or other soft material, so as to be perfectly air or steam tight. Lately, pistons have been made altogether of metal, and, in some cases, from working with less friction, these answer eveu better than others. The next pari to be mentioned is the boiler , which is made of suitable size and strength. The steam passes from the boiler along the pipe, and there, by any suitable cocli or valves, worked by the engine itself, is directed alter nately to the upper and under part of the barrel ; and while it is entering to press on one side of the piston, the waste steam is allowed to escape from the other side, either to the atmosphere, for high pressure engines, or into the condenser, for those of low pres sure; the condenser being always kept at a

low temperature by cold water running into it, and pumped out again by the piston. The supply of steam from the boiler to the cy linder is regulated by a valve placed some where in the pipe, and made obedient to what is called the governor, which may, in truth, be described as a pair of tongs with heavy balls at the ends, to make their opening more energetic, and attached to some turning part of the machine. If the engine move with more than the assigned speed, the balls open or fly asunder beyond their middle station, and, by a simple contrivance, aie then made to act on a valve which contracts the steam lube; on the contrary, with too slow a motion, they collapse, and open the valve The supply of water to the boiler is regulated by a float on the surface of the water in the boiler; which float, on descending to a certain point, by reason of the consumption of water, opens a valve to admit m ire. There is a safely valve, in the boiler, viz , a well-fitted flap or stopper, held against an opening by a weight, but loaded so as to open before danger can arise from the over heating of the w ater. THE PANAMA RAILROAD The following account of this important work is supplied by Col. Hughes, the chief engineer : þÿ The summit of the railroad between the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean has been ascertained to ho only 260 feet above the Pacific, which may he readily reduced to 210 feet by a moderately short cutting. þÿ This will give a gradient not exceeding 30 or 35 feet to the mile, and the gradient will he an uniformly descending one from the summit to both oceans, crossing the stream just high enough to pass this water. Until a very recent period it was supposed that the pass from Solo Nicaragua to Redigo on the Pacific was the lowest pass in the Cordirilleras from the Straits of Behring lo Magellan, but that is now known not strictly to be the fact. The probability is, that the Panama summit is decidedly the lowest. The northern terminus is established on that portion of Simon Bay called Navy Bay, formed by Manziliella Island, which, according to the British Admiralty Charts, may he entered willi 3(5 feet water, and showing i B J8 feet wilhin a short distance of the shore on the main land, near Point Coco Solo. The southern terminus has not yet been determined, and will depend mainly on a minute hydrographical survey, to be made hereafter. þÿ The survey of the route may he said to he essentially finished, and the en-, ginerring parties are to sail for New York from t'hagres on the 3 1st of May, at which place the maps and plans will la drawn, and contracts for

the execution of the work will he let. It. is supposed that the construction of the railroad will commence in the early pnrf of next year. The entire length of the Panama Railroad will be about 4 f English miles. The new summit is 77 feet lower than any known pass in the isthmus before the present party commenced operations, and is nearly 1 1 HI feet less than any reported by Clarella, the French engineer.
